column5: from mother's womb to naked return
column6: Job says he came naked from his mother's womb and will return naked. The saying compresses bodily origin and mortality into the life-course arc that the commentary traces from womb formation to its end.

column5: Spirit made me; breath gives life
column6: Job's interlocutor says God's Spirit made him and the Almighty's breath gives him life. It is a particularly direct Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's formed body followed by enlivening breath.

column5: spirit and breath gathered back
column6: Elihu imagines God gathering back to himself a creature's spirit and breath. This supplies the withdrawal side of the commentary's body-and-breath sequence.

column5: all flesh perishes and returns to dust
column6: The consequence of withdrawn breath is that all flesh dies and humanity returns to dust. It makes the body, breath, and earth sequence explicit before any resurrection answer is supplied.

column5: God knows the frame and remembers dust
column6: The psalm says God knows the human frame and remembers that humans are dust. It ties bodily construction to earthly frailty, supplementing the commentary's formed body and its eventual decline.

column5: dust returns; spirit returns to God
column6: Ecclesiastes separates the body's return to earth from the spirit's return to God. It gives a sharply stated deathward counterpart to the commentary's body-and-breath account and its afterlife horizon.

column5: mortal human made like grass
column6: Isaiah calls a mortal human being like grass. This directly joins the human body and fading vegetation that the commentary treats as one warning about temporary worldly life.

column5: created for incorruption and eternity
column6: Wisdom says God created humanity for incorruption and made it in the likeness of divine eternity. It gives a Jewish counterweight to bodily decay that closely matches the commentary's contrast of worldly life with what endures.

column5: power over life, death, and return
column6: Wisdom attributes authority over life and death to God, including bringing people down to Hades and back. It is a direct Jewish formulation of the creation-to-resurrection inference developed in the commentary.

column5: dust-made body and breath of life
column6: Fourth Ezra says God commanded dust to give Adam, a lifeless body formed by divine hands, then breathed life into him. The retelling explicitly combines the commentary's earth, fashioned body, and breath sequence.

column5: formed, born, lives, dies, and gives account
column6: Avot presents human formation, birth, life, death, and judgment as an involuntary ordered sequence. It is a rabbinic whole-life formulation for the stages the commentary assembles from womb to old age and final reckoning.

column5: those in tombs hear the voice
column6: Jesus says all who are in tombs will hear his voice. It supplies a New Testament voice-to-bodily-resurrection counterpart to the commentary's move from divine speech and formation to the raising of the dead.

column5: come out to divergent judgment
column6: Those who hear come out, to life or judgment according to their deeds. The bodily emergence and divided final outcome develop the resurrection horizon invoked by the commentary.

column5: gives life to dead and calls what is not
column6: Paul characterizes God as giving life to the dead and calling into being things that are not. The paired creation-and-revival formula closely matches the commentary's use of fetal creation as evidence for resurrection.

column5: living soul and life-giving Spirit
column6: Paul rereads Adam's becoming a living soul against the last Adam as life-giving Spirit. This Christian interpretation directly develops the formed-and-breathed human of Genesis into an eschatological body-and-life contrast.

column5: command, trumpet, and dead rising
column6: At the Lord's commanding call, the dead in Christ rise first. It gives a concrete Christian scene of divine sound followed by resurrection, alongside the commentary's recitation and revivification themes.

column5: measure and number of days
column6: The psalmist asks to know the measure and extent of his days. This gives a personal, prayerful analogue to the commentary's understanding of qaddara as a life set to a measure.

column5: remember Creator in days of youth
column6: Ecclesiastes calls for remembering the Creator during youth before the difficult days arrive. It makes youth and later decline an ethical frame, matching the commentary's use of completed youth and old age as life stages.

column5: spirit and breath made by God
column6: Isaiah says that the spirit would fail before God, along with the breaths God has made. The verse joins creaturely frailty with divine authorship of breath, though its immediate context is divine restraint from wrath.

column5: tongue, eyes, ears, mind, understanding
column6: Sirach attributes human tongue, eyes, ears, mind, knowledge, and understanding to God. It offers a sapiential expansion of the commentary's properly ordered body into its sensory and cognitive capacities.

column5: bearing the heavenly image
column6: Paul says believers will bear the image of the heavenly one. It continues his bodily-resurrection argument by moving from an earthly formed humanity toward a transformed eschatological embodiment.

column5: new birth through resurrection to living hope
column6: First Peter blesses God for giving a new birth into living hope through Jesus' resurrection. It extends the commentary's birth-and-revival nexus into a Christian account of renewed life.

column5: earthly tent and enduring divine dwelling
column6: Paul contrasts the destruction of the earthly tent with an enduring dwelling from God. Its body-as-dwelling image makes the commentary's perishable worldly life and lasting future into an explicit Christian contrast.

column5: life as a briefly appearing vapor
column6: James describes present life as vapor that appears briefly and vanishes. It provides a compact ethical analogue to the commentary's warning that worldly life and its flourishing are transient.
